1  BRIEF FACTS AND REASONS FOR DECISION OF THE  CASE 1.

This case has arisen out of FIR No. 641/2006 registered on the complaint of the first informant/complainant Chanderwati wife of Lekh Raj, for the offence punishable under Section 420/34 IPC registered at P.S. Badarpur, on the allegations (as per FIR) that she has known the Accused Chander Shekhar Mishra for the past one and a half years through some common person,
as a property dealer, who had committed the offence of cheating by handing over fake gold biscuits against consideration.

2. It is alleged that on 27.07.2006, she had informed him regarding the sale of his sister's plot and subsequently on 01.08.2006 the Accused Chander Shekhar Mishra had offered her that his partner could bring cheaper gold from Mumbai and if she could arrange a customer for this, they could sell 1 kg of gold for Rs. 7 lakhs (Rs. 10 lakhs being the market value).
He further stated that she would get a commission of Rs. 20,000/-, thereby State Vs. Chander Shekhar Mishra constantly compelling her for arranging a customer.
It was reported that on 07.08.2006, the Accused called his partner Pandey who came to her house and they induced her for hefty commission against the aforesaid deal.
She claimed she had met the two persons at Chandni Chowk area, when the Accused allured her for the purchase of gold.
She then contacted her sister Lajja Devi, who facilitated the deal and the complainant then brought Rs. 5.6 lakhs for purchase of gold.
Thereafter, she along with her niece Manju came to the South Extension area, where both the Accused met them.
Then they came to Ali Gaon Mathura Road, where the Accused Pandey handed over 7 gold biscuits to her and took Rs. 5.6 Lakhs from her.
On checking the gold biscuits were found to be fake and both the Accused persons thereafter could not be found.
On this complaint, the aforesaid FIR was registered.
COURT PROCEEDINGS 3.

Chander Shekhar Mishra (accused facing trial) and (ii) Shiv Asre Pandey (declared Proclaimed Offender during investigation on 07.07.2009).
Cognizance was taken by the Ld. Predecessor vide Order dated 05.09.2009 and the Accused Chander Shekhar was summoned.

The supplementary report was filed in this matter with the FSL result of the biscuits handed over by the complainant to the IO State Vs. Chander Shekhar Mishra vide seizure memo Ex PW1/ B, along with certain other documents.

sentences.text: He in return offered to get her 2 kg gold (at the rate of Rs. 7 lakhs) stating that the market value of the same is Rs. 10 lacs per kg.
Accused Chander Shekhar also told her that if the deal is materialized, he would get enough money to get the house repaired.
On 07.08.2006, Accused had asked the deponent to come to a temple at Chandni Chowk.
She reached there at about 3.30 pm where the Accused along with the other person named Pandey and one more person were present.
The Accused told her that she should arrange money from her sister and had showed her 2-3 pieces of gold biscuits measuring around 2 inch, as sample.
The Complainant claims that she was offered a drink, after consuming which she got influenced and opted to buy the gold.
Next morning, she told the Accused Chander Shekhar that she wanted to buy gold and subsequently, the Accused along with Pandey (PO) came in an auto at Kalkaji Depot and met her there.
From there she went to South Extension along with the Accused by auto.
Both of them kept sitting in the auto and the deponent went inside the house of her sister Lajja Devi i.e. H. No. 216, Masjid Mod, South Extension.
She asked for a sum of Rs. 5.5 lakhs from her sister for one day, which she gave to her.
She also added Rs.10,000/- from her savings to the amount.
She has stated that the daughter of her sister Manju accompanied her on the insistence of her sister, as she was carrying a huge sum of money.

From there they went to the Accused persons who were sitting in State Vs. Chander Shekhar Mishra the auto and the complainant handed over a sum of Rs.5.60 lacs to the Accused Chander Shekhar, who gave her 7 gold biscuits.
He asked her to wait stating that he would bring the remaining biscuits.
The Accused however, left from there.
The deponent along with Manju kept on waiting till 8.30 pm, but they never turned up.
When she called the Accused Chander Shekhar, he told her that it was a quite late and that he would bring remaining pieces of gold biscuit on the next date.
Thereafter, the Accused could not be contacted.
When she met the wife of the Accused Chander Shekhar, she told her that Chander Shekhar had not returned to the house since 11.08.2006.
On 17.08.2006, the Complainant gave the complaint to the police Ex.PW1/A and handed over the seven biscuits which were seized by the police vide seizure memo Ex.PW1/B.
The accused was arrested eventually vide Arrest Memo Ex.PW1/C bearing the signatures of the complainant.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS 20.
At the threshold, the ingredients of Section 420 IPC have to be borne in mind.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It has been further held in the context in Devender Kumar (supra) that it is not necessary that a false pretense should be made in express words by the Accused, as it may be inferred from all the circumstances, including the conduct of the Accused, in obtaining the property.

It is also a settled principle of law as laid down in Vijay Kumar Ghai v State of WB [(2022) 7 SCC 124] that for the purpose of cheating there has to be culpable intention at the time of making the promise, only then failure on the part of the Accused to keep his promise, can be construed as an offence punishable under Section 420 IPC.

sentences.text: In the case at hand, the Prosecutrix/ the Complainant has reiterated her case by way of narration of events in her deposition recorded as PW1, whereby she has specifically explained the systematic manner in which the Accused had induced her into shelling out a huge sum of money to the tune of Rs 5.6 lakhs, upon the assurance of a deal for sale of gold biscuits, with the promise of consideration, which could be later used by the Complainant to repair her own dilapidated house.

The witness mentioned of a meeting prior to the relevant date, when she was shown the sample of the gold biscuits offered for sale, with she having been persuaded into believing the representation of the Accused, that what was being offered against consideration of a hefty amount, was genuine.

It was the Accused as per PW1 who had offered to sell the biscuits projected as of gold, asking her to arrange the consideration for the same out of the proceeds of the sale of a plot of land by her sister (examined as PW6), which information was shared by the Complainant with the Accused under confidence.

Under the aforesaid representation of offering a genuine deal for sale of the purported gold biscuits in possession of the Accused, with samples being shown in advance, the Accused induced the Complainant to avail of the money to the tune of Rs. 5.5 lakhs from her sister and upon adding a further amount of Rs. 10,000/- from her personal savings towards the deal, which was handed over to the Accused, who was accompanied by his Associate (already PO as above noted).
The Accused however gave 7 biscuits, projected as made State Vs. Chander Shekhar Mishra of gold to the Complainant, who was accompanied by her niece (examined as PW7) for the aforesaid meeting.
He then left the spot after taking the money, assuring to return with more biscuits, but failed to do so.

Upon suspicion, the Complainant followed up by reaching the house of the Accused,
where she met with his wife, who was herself clueless about his whereabouts since 11.8.2006.

Upon further suspicion building over the genuineness of the deal, the witness PW1 along with PW6 (as per the testimony of the latter), went to a jeweler to confirm, who disclosed that the biscuits were fake.

PW1 has proved to have lodged the complaint Ex PW1/A on 17.8.2006 with the police and to have handed over the 'gold' biscuits to the police vide seizure memo Ex PW1/B.
22.

It is striking to note, that despite opportunities, neither was PW1 nor were the other material witnesses, inter-alia, PW7 (the niece of the complainant who confirmed the events as deposed to have transpired on the relevant date of the meeting inter-se the Accused and her aunt and of exchange of fake biscuits against consideration availed by PW1 from the mother of PW7, vide her testimony) cross examined by the Accused.

Even in the cross examination of PW6 (sister of the Complainant), there is no suggestion refuting the claim of she having helped the Complainant with the consideration amount she required to facilitate the deal for sale of the gold biscuits.

Further, the witness PW4, nephew of the Complainant PW1, too has in his State Vs. Chander Shekhar Mishra statement recorded on 8.1.2015 proved that he was a witness to the recording of the statement of Complainant (Ex PW1/A) by the police and also a witness to the seizure of the fake gold biscuits by the police from the Complainant (memo being Ex PW1/B).
He also accompanied the Complainant to the Police Station and later to the house of the Accused, where he was not found.

It is glaring to note, that even this witness was not cross examined by the Accused.
23.

Amongst all the witnesses examined by the Prosecution, it is essentially the IO/ ACP Virender Singh (PW14) who has been cross examined by the Accused, in whose statement he has been questioned about the presence of independent witnesses at the time of seizure of the metallic biscuits produced by the Complainant.

The very fact that the Accused has neither by way of cross State vs Chander Shekhar on 15 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/12365547/
7 examination, nor in his plea recorded under Section 313 Cr.P.C. or even by way of leading any independent evidence in defence, denied the claim of being in possession of certain biscuits, which were later under a transaction handed over to the Complainant by him, renders the aforesaid questioning over absence of independent witnesses to their recovery from the Complainant inconsequential, as the chain of transfer of the case property has not been in dispute at all.

Thus,
there is no evidence to suggest that the same was either not initially possessed by the Accused, or never delivered to the Complainant, from whom it was eventually recovered vide memo Ex PW1/B.
Even otherwise State Vs. Chander Shekhar Mishra it is trite law as held in Ambika Prasad v State (Delhi Administration) [(2000) 2 SCC 646)] that it is usually very difficult to find independent public persons who would readily want to depose as witnesses or assist in investigation.

entities.text: Ambika Prasad v State (Delhi Administration) [(2000) 2 SCC 646)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
It was observed that 'if the testimonies of the witnesses deposing are otherwise trustworthy, the prosecution's case cannot fail simply because no public witnesses were examined'.
24.
Despite having sought the opportunity to lead evidence in defence initially, the Accused subsequently forfeited it.

The forensic scrutiny of the biscuits/ case property (Ex P 1 Colly) by the FSL has confirmed vide its report Ex PW9/A that the biscuits were made up of 85 % Copper and 11 % Zinc, 'which indicates that the same were made of Brass' and that the same were having only a coating of Gold.
The Accused has not posed any questions during the cross examination of the witnesses concerning the aforesaid report/ findings.
There is absolutely no defence put up to the claims in the Prosecution version/ narration of events.

It is a settled principle of law as observed by Hon'ble Supreme Court in Raj Kumar Singh @ Raju @ Batya v State of Rajasthan [ AIR 2013 SC 3150] that the "Accused has a duty to furnish explanation in his statements under Section 313 Cr.P.C. regarding any incriminating material that has been produced against him".

entities.text: Raj Kumar Singh @ Raju @ Batya v State of Rajasthan [ AIR 2013 SC 3150]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It was further held that though the Accused may choose to stay silent when confronted with such evidence, in such an event adverse inference could be drawn against the Accused, as may be State Vs. Chander Shekhar Mishra permissible under law.
In the instant case, the Accused has responded to the evidence stating that the same is a 'matter of record'.
This plea can by no means be construed as one refuting/ questioning the incriminating material on record.

There is rather an element of evasiveness in the response, when the Accused states that the evidence put to him is the one which is one record, with no further claims questioning its veracity, genuineness or creditworthiness.

25. The Accused Chander Prakash is on the basis of the evidence led by the Prosecution, proved to have systematically induced the Complainant/PW1 by making a dishonest representation concerning the bona fides of an offer for sale of what was posed as genuine 'gold biscuits' and to have pursued and persuaded her into entering into the said deal and making her agree to part with consideration towards the purchase of what turned out to be nothing but 'metallic pieces' made up of brass.

It has been held in Alpic Finance Ltd. V P Sadasivan (2001) 3 SCC 513 by the Hon'ble Supreme Court that it must be shown that there existed a fraudulent and dishonest intention 'at the time of commission of the offence'.

entities.text: Alpic Finance Ltd. V P Sadasivan (2001) 3 SCC 513
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
In the instant case, the intention to defraud is also proved to have existed from the beginning considering the Complainant was shown certain samples of the pieces being offered in a meeting preceding the eventual meet for striking the deal and for change of hands of the pieces and the consideration amount, and despite knowing that what was in the State Vs. Chander Shekhar Mishra offing for sale were metallic pieces, the Accused intentionally made a false representation towards sale of 'gold biscuits' to the Complainant, to induce her into delivering State vs Chander Shekhar on 15 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/12365547/
8
the monetary worth quoted.
CONCLUSION 26.

Accordingly, for the afore-discussed reasons, the Prosecution has successfully brought home the charges against the Accused for the offence punishable under Section 420 IPC, on the basis of unflinching, credible and uncontroverted evidence, proving the case against the Accused beyond all reasonable doubts.
The Accused, thus, is hereby convicted for the offence punishable under Section 420 IPC.

The Accused had admitted the genuineness of the FIR bearing no. 641/06 registered at P.S. Badarpur with his statement recorded under Section 294 Cr.P.C. on 12.9.2017.
State Vs. Chander Shekhar Mishra 8.
Statement of the Accused was recorded under Section 313 Cr.P.C. wherein he was confronted with all the incriminating evidence, to which his response was recorded.
He has specified that each of the incriminating facts proven against him are a 'matter of record', further claiming that he has been falsely implicated at the instance of the complainant and all the witnesses deposing for the Prosecution are interested witnesses.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
At the threshold, the ingredients of Section 420 IPC have to be borne in mind.
It has been held by the Hon'ble Apex Court in Devender Kumar Singla v Baldev Krishan Singla [(2005) 9 SCC 15]
that essential ingredients to attract Section 420 IPC are (i) cheating; (ii) dishonest inducement to deliver property or to make, alter or destroy any valuable security or anything which is sealed or signed or is capable of being converted into valuable security;
and (iii) mens rea of the Accused at the time of making the inducement.
It is also a settled principle of law as laid down in Vijay Kumar Ghai v State of WB [(2022) 7 SCC 124] that for the purpose of cheating there has to be culpable intention at the time of making the promise, only then failure on the part of the Accused to keep his promise, can be construed as an offence punishable under Section 420 IPC.
State Vs. Chander Shekhar Mishra State vs Chander Shekhar on 15 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/12365547/
6 21.
The very fact that the Accused has neither by way of cross State vs Chander Shekhar on 15 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/12365547/
7 examination, nor in his plea recorded under Section 313 Cr.P.C. or even by way of leading any independent evidence in defence, denied the claim of being in possession of certain biscuits, which were later under a transaction handed over to the Complainant by him, renders the aforesaid questioning over absence of independent witnesses to their recovery from the Complainant inconsequential, as the chain of transfer of the case property has not been in dispute at all.
Thus,
there is no evidence to suggest that the same was either not initially possessed by the Accused, or never delivered to the Complainant, from whom it was eventually recovered vide memo Ex PW1/B.
Even otherwise State Vs. Chander Shekhar Mishra it is trite law as held in Ambika Prasad v State (Delhi Administration) [(2000) 2 SCC 646)] that it is usually very difficult to find independent public persons who would readily want to depose as witnesses or assist in investigation.
The forensic scrutiny of the biscuits/ case property (Ex P 1 Colly) by the FSL has confirmed vide its report Ex PW9/A that the biscuits were made up of 85 % Copper and 11 % Zinc, 'which indicates that the same were made of Brass' and that the same were having only a coating of Gold.
The Accused has not posed any questions during the cross examination of the witnesses concerning the aforesaid report/ findings.
There is absolutely no defence put up to the claims in the Prosecution version/ narration of events.
It is a settled principle of law as observed by Hon'ble Supreme Court in Raj Kumar Singh @ Raju @ Batya v State of Rajasthan [ AIR 2013 SC 3150] that the "Accused has a duty to furnish explanation in his statements under Section 313 Cr.P.C. regarding any incriminating material that has been produced against him".
In the instant case, the Accused has responded to the evidence stating that the same is a 'matter of record'.
This plea can by no means be construed as one refuting/ questioning the incriminating material on record.
There is rather an element of evasiveness in the response, when the Accused states that the evidence put to him is the one which is one record, with no further claims questioning its veracity, genuineness or creditworthiness.
25. The Accused Chander Prakash is on the basis of the evidence led by the Prosecution, proved to have systematically induced the Complainant/PW1 by making a dishonest representation concerning the bona fides of an offer for sale of what was posed as genuine 'gold biscuits' and to have pursued and persuaded her into entering into the said deal and making her agree to part with consideration towards the purchase of what turned out to be nothing but 'metallic pieces' made up of brass.
It has been held in Alpic Finance Ltd. V P Sadasivan (2001) 3 SCC 513 by the Hon'ble Supreme Court that it must be shown that there existed a fraudulent and dishonest intention 'at the time of commission of the offence'.
In the instant case, the intention to defraud is also proved to have existed from the beginning considering the Complainant was shown certain samples of the pieces being offered in a meeting preceding the eventual meet for striking the deal and for change of hands of the pieces and the consideration amount, and despite knowing that what was in the State Vs. Chander Shekhar Mishra offing for sale were metallic pieces, the Accused intentionally made a false representation towards sale of 'gold biscuits' to the Complainant, to induce her into delivering State vs Chander Shekhar on 15 March, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/12365547/
8
Accordingly, for the afore-discussed reasons, the Prosecution has successfully brought home the charges against the Accused for the offence punishable under Section 420 IPC, on the basis of unflinching, credible and uncontroverted evidence, proving the case against the Accused beyond all reasonable doubts.
opennyai_summary.arguments: It has been further held in the context in Devender Kumar (supra) that it is not necessary that a false pretense should be made in express words by the Accused, as it may be inferred from all the circumstances, including the conduct of the Accused, in obtaining the property.
